item.title: Flathead Lake Life: Lakeside, Somers, and Bigfork, Compared
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Three communities on the same shoreline, three completely different daily rhythms. A practical look at marina access, dining and services, the drive to Kalispell, and what summer versus winter actually feels like in Lakeside, Somers, and Bigfork.
item.content:encoded:
Most people who call me about Flathead Lake say some version of the same thing: "We want to be on the lake."

Then I ask one question that usually changes the search entirely.

Which lake?

Not a trick. Flathead Lake is nearly 200 square miles of water, and the communities ringing its northern half share a shoreline and almost nothing else. Lakeside, Somers, and Bigfork sit within twenty minutes of each other. Their daily rhythms are three separate lives.

Here's the honest comparison, amenity by amenity.

The Drive to Kalispell Is the First Filter

Start here, because it's the one thing you can't renovate.

Somers sits at the very head of the lake, closest in of the three. The run up US Highway 93 into Kalispell is short enough that plenty of people do it daily without thinking about it — groceries, Logan Health, the airport, all comfortably inside a normal errand loop.

Lakeside is a few miles further down the west shore on the same highway. Still an easy commute, but you feel the difference in winter when 93 gets weather and the shoulder-season traffic thins out. Everything in Kalispell is reachable; nothing in Kalispell is casual.

Bigfork is the outlier. You're crossing to the northeast corner of the lake, and the drive runs closer to half an hour depending on where you are in the community. That distance is exactly why Bigfork developed its own downtown instead of borrowing Kalispell's.

If someone in the household commutes to Kalispell five days a week, that gap matters more than any feature list.

Water Access: Not All Lakefront Is the Same

All three have marina access. What that access looks like is different.

Lakeside has a working marina and public access right in the middle of town, plus Volunteer Park for swimming and picnicking. West shore frontage tends to be steeper — you're often looking down at the water from above rather than walking out onto it, which is worth understanding before you fall in love with a listing photo.

Somers anchors the shallow north bay. Somers Bay has a marina, and Somers Beach State Park opened relatively recently at the north end, which added real public shoreline where there wasn't much before. The bay is warmer and calmer than open water — great for paddling and swimming, less ideal if you're chasing deep-water moorage for a big boat.

Bigfork has a protected harbor at the mouth of the Swan River, which is a genuine advantage on a lake that can build serious chop. There's marina moorage, and the Wild Mile stretch of the Swan is a known whitewater run right at the edge of town.

The practical question isn't "is it on the lake." It's whether you're getting a dock, deeded access, a shared association beach, or a view and a ten-minute drive to a public ramp. Those four things carry very different price tags and very different ownership headaches.

Dining, Shopping, and What's Open in February

This is the split most buyers underestimate.

Bigfork has the deepest downtown of the three. Electric Avenue runs galleries, restaurants, and shops, and the Bigfork Summer Playhouse has been a fixture for decades. Eagle Bend Golf Club is right there. You can eat out, buy a gift, see a show, and play a round without leaving town.

Lakeside has a compact commercial strip along the highway — a grocery stop, a handful of restaurants and a brewery, the basics covered. Enough that you're not driving to Kalispell for milk.

Somers is the smallest footprint of the three. A few well-known spots, a general store, and not much else — the tradeoff for being closest to Kalispell's full retail base.

Then ask the follow-up: what stays open off-season? Every lake town in America thins out after Labor Day, and the Flathead is no exception. Bigfork carries more year-round activity than the other two. In Lakeside and Somers, winter is genuinely quiet — which is a feature or a bug depending entirely on who you are.

Summer Crowds Versus Winter Quiet

June through August, the whole west shore is busy. Highway 93 carries Glacier National Park traffic, cherry stands go up along the shoreline, and the boat ramps have lines on weekends.

Come October, it empties out. If you're buying based on an August visit, go back in February before you write an offer. I've had more than one client realize they'd fallen for a season rather than a place.

Worth knowing: Blacktail Mountain Ski Area sits in the hills above Lakeside — a small, uncrowded hill that gives the west shore a winter identity. On the Bigfork side, the Jewel Basin Hiking Area trailhead is a short drive up, and the Great Northern Historical Trail connects Somers toward Kalispell for riding and walking.

Schools and Districts

Bigfork operates its own K–12 district. Somers and Lakeside share an elementary and middle school district, with high school students heading into Kalispell.

Boundaries and enrollment policies change, so confirm current lines directly with the district office for any specific address before you make a decision based on them.

So Which One?

Rough shorthand, and treat it as a starting point rather than a verdict:

  • Somers if the commute is the priority and you want bay water and quiet.
  • Lakeside if you want highway convenience, a ski hill in your backyard, and west-shore views.
  • Bigfork if you want a real downtown and protected harbor access, and the longer drive doesn't bother you.

Here's the question I'd actually sit with: on a random Tuesday in November — not a July Saturday — what do you want your evening to look like? Answer that honestly and one of these three usually picks itself.

If you're weighing a move to the lake and want a straight, no-pitch read on which community fits how you actually live, I'm glad to walk through it with you. item.title: The Step-Up Basis: What Selling an Inherited Montana Home Really Costs
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Inherited a home in the Flathead Valley? The step-up in basis means the tax bill is usually far smaller than families fear. Here's how it works, why a date-of-death appraisal matters, and the records to gather now.
item.content:encoded:
The Step-Up Basis: What Selling an Inherited Montana Home Really Costs

Here's the question I hear most often from heirs, usually asked quietly, sometimes with a little dread behind it: "If we sell Mom's house, how much are we going to lose to taxes?"

And here's what almost nobody has explained to them before they ask: usually far less than they fear. Often close to nothing.

The reason is a tax rule called the step-up in basis — and if you've inherited a home in Kalispell, Whitefish, or anywhere in the Flathead Valley, it may be the single most important piece of the picture. It's also the one most families learn about last.

First, the required disclaimer, and I mean it: I'm a real estate agent, not a CPA or an attorney. What follows is general information to help you ask better questions. Your specific numbers need to come from your tax professional.

What "basis" means — and why it resets

When you sell a property, capital gains tax is calculated on the difference between what you sell it for and your basis — roughly, what was paid for it, plus certain improvements.

Now think about a Flathead Valley home your parents bought decades ago. A house purchased in Kalispell in 1992 for $110,000 might be worth $600,000 today. If your parents sold it themselves, that gap is the gain the tax math starts from.

But when a property passes to heirs, something different happens. In most cases, the basis resets — it "steps up" — to the property's fair market value on the date of death.

Read that again, because it changes everything: the decades of appreciation that happened during your parents' lifetime generally aren't taxed as your gain when you inherit. Your starting line moves to the value on the day they passed.

So if the home was worth $600,000 at the date of death and the estate sells it a few months later for $615,000, the taxable gain isn't $505,000. It's in the neighborhood of $15,000 — before selling costs, which reduce it further. For many families, once commissions and closing costs come out, the taxable gain on a reasonably prompt sale is small or effectively zero.

That's the fear most heirs carry into this process, dissolved by one rule. Which is exactly why it frustrates me that so few families hear about it early.

Why the date-of-death appraisal matters — even if you're not selling yet

Here's the practical catch: a step-up is only as good as your ability to document the stepped-up value.

That's what a date-of-death appraisal is for. A licensed appraiser values the property as of the date of death — not as of today, not as of whenever you get around to it. That number becomes the anchor for everything downstream: the estate's records, the eventual sale, and the tax return that follows.

Two things I tell every personal representative:

Get it done early. Appraisers can work retrospectively, but the further you get from the date of death — especially in a market that moves like the Flathead's — the harder the reconstruction becomes. An appraisal ordered promptly is clean evidence. One ordered three years later is an argument.

Get it even if you plan to keep the house. Some heirs hold the property for years — as a family cabin, a rental, an eventual retirement landing spot. The step-up still applies, but only the value at death gets the reset. Everything the home gains after that date is potential future gain, measured against the date-of-death number. If that number was never documented, you've made your future self's tax problem much harder than it needed to be.

One more nuance worth knowing: inherited property is generally treated as long-term for capital gains purposes, no matter how briefly you've held it. Sell six weeks after probate opens and the gain — if there is one — typically gets long-term treatment. Again: confirm with your CPA.

The records a personal representative should gather now

If you're serving as personal representative of a Montana estate, here's the file I'd build before the house question even comes up. Think of it as pre-mission preparation — done early, it makes every later step calmer.

The date-of-death appraisal. Records of major improvements made after the date of death, since those can adjust the basis going forward. Every invoice from the sale process itself — repairs, cleanout, staging, commissions, closing costs — because selling expenses matter in the final math. Property tax and insurance records showing the estate maintained the home. And the probate paperwork establishing your authority to sell, which the title company will ask for anyway.

None of this is complicated. All of it is easier to collect in month one than in month fourteen — and your CPA and attorney will thank you for it.

What this means for the timing decision

Families often assume they need to rush a sale "before taxes eat the value," or hold the property for some magic period. The step-up quietly removes most of that pressure. Because the basis resets at death, a prompt, orderly sale usually produces little taxable gain — and holding longer doesn't improve the tax picture, it just starts the clock on new appreciation.

Which means the real questions become practical ones: What does the home need before market? Who's handling the contents? How do out-of-state heirs stay informed? Those are solvable, one phase at a time — and they're a subject I've covered before and will again.

So here's the question worth sitting with: if the tax fear isn't the obstacle you thought it was — what's actually holding the decision in place?

item.title: Well and Septic in the Flathead Valley: The Due Diligence Most Buyers Skip
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Buying a home on a well and septic in the Flathead Valley? Here's the due diligence checklist most buyers skip — well logs, water testing, septic inspections, and how to write the contingency right.
item.content:encoded:
Well and Septic in the Flathead Valley: The Due Diligence Most Buyers Skip

Here's a question most buyers never think to ask until it's too late: if the home you're about to buy sits outside city limits, do you actually know where your water comes from — and where it goes when you're done with it?

In the Flathead Valley, once you leave the city services of Kalispell, Whitefish, or Columbia Falls, the answer is almost always a private well and a septic system. And if you're moving from town — or relocating from out of state — there's a good chance you've never owned either one.

That's not a problem. Skipping the due diligence on them is.

I brief my buyers on wells and septic the same way I'd brief any mission: know the terrain before you commit. Here's the checklist.

Start With the Well Log

Every drilled well in Montana should have a well log on file — a record created when the well was drilled that tells you the depth, the static water level, the flow rate at completion, and what the driller punched through to get there.

You can look these up yourself through the Montana Bureau of Mines and Geology's Ground Water Information Center (GWIC) database. It's free, it's public, and it takes about ten minutes.

What you're looking for: how deep is the well, when was it drilled, and what did it produce at the time? A well drilled in 1978 producing 8 gallons per minute isn't automatically a problem — but it's a data point you want before you're under contract, not after.

If there's no log on file, that's not an automatic walk-away either. But it moves testing from "recommended" to "non-negotiable."

Test the Flow, Then Test the Water

The well log tells you what the well did the day it was drilled. It doesn't tell you what it does today. That's what a flow test is for.

A proper flow test runs the well for an extended period — not thirty seconds at the kitchen tap — and measures whether it sustains production. Wells can slow down over decades. Aquifers shift. You want to know the well keeps up with a family's real usage: laundry, showers, irrigation, all on the same Saturday.

Water quality is the second half. At minimum, test for coliform bacteria and nitrates. Depending on the property and the area, your inspector may recommend adding tests for things like arsenic or other naturally occurring minerals — some parts of Montana have them, and you won't taste them.

Budget-wise, think of flow and quality testing together as a few hundred dollars, give or take, depending on how many panels you run. Against the price of a home — and the cost of drilling a new well, which can run well into five figures — it's the cheapest insurance in the transaction.

The Septic System: Pump It, Inspect It, Pull the Permit

Here's what most people get wrong about septic: they treat the inspection as optional because the seller says "it's never had a problem."

A septic system can be quietly failing for years before anyone notices a problem above ground. The only way to know is a real inspection — which means the tank gets pumped and a qualified inspector actually looks at the tank, the baffles, and the drainfield's condition. An inspection without pumping is a guess.

While that's being scheduled, pull the paperwork. Septic permits in this county run through the Flathead City-County Health Department. The permit record tells you when the system was installed, what it was designed for, and whether it was permitted at all.

That last part matters more than you'd think. A three-bedroom home with a septic system permitted for two bedrooms is a real conversation — about capacity, about future resale, and sometimes about price.

Write the Contingency Like You Mean It

All of this only protects you if it's in the contract.

Your inspection contingency should specifically cover well and septic — with enough time to actually complete the work. Pumping and inspecting a septic tank, running a flow test, and getting water samples through a lab isn't a 48-hour turnaround, especially in the busy season when every inspector in the valley is booked.

Talk to your agent about the timeline before you write the offer, not after. And if the tests turn something up, the contingency is what gives you room to negotiate a repair, a credit, or — if it comes to it — a clean exit with your earnest money intact.

This is also the place for the standard disclaimer: I'm a real estate agent, not an attorney. For contract language questions, consult your attorney.

The October Problem

Why does all this matter so much? Because the failure mode is predictable.

Buyer closes in July. Skips the flow test because the water ran fine during the showing. Skips the septic inspection because the seller's disclosure said no known issues. Then October arrives, the house is full, the laundry is running daily — and the well can't keep up, or the drainfield backs up after the first hard freeze.

Now it's not a negotiation. It's a repair bill. And the leverage you had under contract is gone.

Due diligence isn't about distrusting anyone. It's about knowing exactly what you're buying before your name is on it. That's how I run every transaction — no surprises, no assumptions, everything verified.

Before You Write That Offer

So here's the question worth sitting with: if the home you're looking at is on a well and septic, can you say — with evidence, not assurances — that both systems will do their job for the next ten years?

If the answer is "I'm not sure," that's exactly the conversation to have before you're under contract. item.title: Divorcing With Kids in the Flathead: Timing the House Around the School Year
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: School starts in days. For divorcing parents in Kalispell and Whitefish, here's how the house decision interacts with school districts, custody schedules, and listing timing — and the one conversation to have before anything goes on the market.
item.content:encoded:
Divorcing With Kids in the Flathead: Timing the House Around the School Year

School starts in the Flathead Valley in about a week. If you're a divorcing parent, you already know that — because the school calendar has quietly become one more thing attached to the house question.

Here's what most people in your situation are actually asking, even if they haven't said it out loud: Can the kids stay in their school? And what does that mean for what we do with the house?

Those are two different questions. Most couples treat them as one, and that's where the avoidable mistakes happen.

The school district question comes first — not the house question

Keeping your kids in their current school doesn't automatically require keeping the current house. It requires an address inside the district boundary — or, in some cases, an approved out-of-district enrollment. Kalispell, Whitefish, Columbia Falls, Bigfork, Somers-Lakeside — each district draws its own lines, and in parts of the valley those lines run closer to your street than you'd guess.

So before anyone declares "we can't sell, the kids need their school," it's worth asking a narrower question: what would it take for at least one parent to live inside the boundary? Sometimes that's the current house. Sometimes it's a rental eight blocks away. Sometimes it's a smaller purchase that one income can actually carry.

The families who navigate this well figure out the school answer first, then let the house decision follow from it — not the other way around.

Why the calendar matters more in a divorce sale

In an ordinary sale, listing timing is a pricing conversation. In a divorce sale with kids, it's also a stability conversation. A move over winter break lands differently than a move in the third week of September. A closing that forces a mid-semester school change is the kind of detail a Montana parenting plan discussion can end up caring about.

That's why some divorcing families in the valley list in the fall on purpose. It sounds backwards — everyone hears that spring is the season — but a fall listing can put closing and moving inside the semester break, give both parents the school year to settle their next housing, and let the family start the following school year with everything already decided. Fall buyers in Kalispell and Whitefish also tend to be fewer but more serious, which matters when you'd rather have one clean transaction than a parade of showings through a house where kids are doing homework.

I'm not telling you fall is the answer. I'm telling you the listing date is a decision, not a default — and in a divorce, it should be made looking at the school calendar and the custody schedule, not just the market chart.

Custody schedules and showings: plan it like logistics, because it is

A house on the market gets shown, photographed, inspected, and appraised. With a custody schedule in play, every one of those events lands on somebody's parenting time.

The couples who keep this low-conflict handle it the way I'd handle any operation: agree on the rules before the first showing, in writing. Which days are available for showings. How much notice each parent gets. Who handles the house on their days. What the kids are told, and by whom. Where the pets go.

None of that is complicated. All of it prevents the 8 p.m. phone call that turns a scheduling hiccup into a court filing. As a neutral third party, part of my job is being the one who communicates with both spouses on the same protocol — same information, same time, no side channels — so the house doesn't become another front.

The one conversation to have before anything goes on the market

Before a sign goes in the yard — before you even pick an agent — talk to your attorney about how the sale interacts with your case. A few specifics worth raising: whether the timing of listing and closing fits the parenting plan you're negotiating, how proceeds will be held and divided at closing, and whether any temporary orders in your case affect listing, showing, or accepting an offer.

I'm not an attorney, and nothing here is legal advice — Montana parenting plans and property division are exactly the things to run through your lawyer. But I can tell you from the real estate side: the sales that go smoothly are the ones where the legal timeline and the listing timeline were lined up on purpose, early. The painful ones are where the house got ahead of the case.

What this looks like when it's done right

A clear phase plan: school decision, legal green light, prep, list, close — each with a date. Both spouses briefed the same way at the same time. Showings scheduled around the custody calendar instead of against it. A closing date chosen with the school calendar in view. No surprises, because surprises are the enemy.

Divorce is hard enough without the house becoming the battlefield. Handled with discipline, it's just a transaction — one with a start date, an end date, and two people who can both live with the result.

So here's the question worth sitting with tonight: if the school year is the clock, what would the right timeline for your house actually look like — and have you and your attorney lined it up yet?

item.title: Kalispell Market Update: The Late-Summer Standoff
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: New listings in Kalispell fell again in mid-August, homes are sitting 110 days, and asking prices are still climbing. Here's the standoff shaping the Flathead Valley market right now — and how to play it whether you're buying or selling.
item.content:encoded:
If you've been watching the Kalispell and Whitefish market this month and thinking "something doesn't add up," you're reading it right. Inventory is shrinking. Homes are sitting longer. And asking prices are going up anyway. Those three things aren't supposed to happen at the same time. When they do, it means the market has settled into a standoff — sellers holding their number, buyers holding their ground, and both sides waiting to see who blinks first as summer winds down. It's Monday. Numbers first, then the read.

The Numbers: Mid-August 2026

Here's the most recent data for Kalispell and the surrounding market, covering July 16 through August 16, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, mid-August 2026 period): New listings came in at 93 — down another 12.3% from the prior period. That follows the 36% drop we saw at the start of the month. Fresh inventory isn't just slowing; it's drying up on schedule, the way it does every year once the back-to-school calendar takes over. Active inventory sits at 511 properties, down about 1% month over month. The summer stack has crested and is slowly thinning. Days on market for active listings stretched to 110, up 6% from the prior period. The homes still on the market are the ones that have been sitting — and they're sitting longer. Price changes: 155 listings cut or adjusted their price this period, up 18.3%. Nearly one in three active listings has moved its number. Remember that stat — it matters more than any other one here. And yet: the average list price on active inventory rose to $950,000 (up 1.6%), and average asking price per square foot jumped to $408, up 15% from the prior period. On rates: the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.67% as of August 13, 2026, down slightly from 6.69% the week before, with the 15-year at 5.96% (source: Freddie Mac PMMS, August 13, 2026). Rates have been parked in the mid-6s for weeks — stable, not helpful.

Wait — Prices Are Up 15%?

No. And this is where most people misread the data. That $408-per-square-foot number describes what's asking, not what's selling. When entry-level and mid-range homes go under contract and don't get replaced by new listings — which is exactly what a 12% drop in new inventory does in August — the leftover pool skews toward the expensive end. Lakefront, acreage, the big log home on the hill. The average rises because the mix changed, not because your house gained 15% in thirty days. The honest read is the opposite of what the headline number suggests: 155 price reductions in one month is the market telling sellers, one listing at a time, that the asking prices are ahead of the buyers. That's the real signal. The rest is math doing what math does when the cheap homes leave the pool. This is why I keep saying: don't price your home off a portal average. Price it off what actually closed in your neighborhood in the last 60 days.

What This Means If You're Selling

If your home has been sitting past that 110-day average, you're not "waiting for the right buyer." You're in the price-reduction cohort — you just haven't made it official yet. The listings that sell in this market are the ones priced at the market on day one, while the 30% doing serial price cuts follow the market down and end up netting less than if they'd started right. Here's the part working in your favor: your competition is evaporating. New listings are down double digits and will keep falling through fall. A well-priced, well-presented home in September faces less competition than at any point since May. If you missed the summer window, don't panic-list at a stale number — reposition once, correctly, and let the thin inventory do its work.

What This Means If You're Buying

A standoff favors the patient side — and right now, that's you. One hundred fifty-five price reductions is 155 sellers who've already admitted their number was wrong. Homes at 110+ days on market have sellers doing math at the kitchen table every night. That's where negotiation room lives: seller credits, rate buydowns, inspection concessions that didn't exist in June. And a rate note worth doing the arithmetic on: 6.67% isn't the rate you'll have forever — it's the rate you'll have until the first refinance window opens. The price you negotiate in a standoff, though, is permanent. Buyers who wait for rates to drop will re-enter the market alongside everyone else who had the same idea, and the leverage you have this fall goes with them.

The Bottom Line

The mid-August market isn't hot and it isn't broken. It's a standoff — thinning inventory holding prices up on paper, longer market times and a wave of price cuts pulling them down in practice. Sellers who price to the closed data (not the asking averages) still sell. Buyers willing to engage with a 100-day listing instead of waiting for a unicorn are getting terms nobody got in spring. Both of those moves require knowing your specific street, not the valley-wide average. That's a fifteen-minute conversation. So here's the question worth sitting with this week: if you're selling, do you actually know what closed near you in the last 60 days — or are you anchored to a number from June? And if you're buying, which of those 110-day listings would you look at differently if you knew the seller had already cut twice? item.title: The Quiet Sale: Why Discretion Wins in Real Estate
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: Not every Flathead Valley home sale belongs on the front page. Here's what a discreet sale actually looks like — pre-market preparation, controlled showings, and information that never leaks — and who tends to need one.
item.content:encoded:
The Quiet Sale: Why Discretion Wins in Real Estate

Here's a question most sellers never think to ask: who needs to know your home is for sale — and who doesn't?

For the average listing, the answer is "everyone." Maximum exposure, maximum eyeballs, maximum offers. That's the standard playbook, and for most homes in Kalispell and Whitefish, it's the right one.

But not every sale is average. Before real estate, I spent years in the Army and then in protective services work for the US government, and in that world, information discipline wasn't a courtesy — it was the job. What got said, to whom, and when was managed deliberately, because loose information created real risk for real people.

Some home sales deserve exactly the same handling. Here's what a quiet sale actually looks like, and how to know if you need one.

Who actually needs a discreet sale

More people than you'd think — and most of them don't realize it until the chatter starts.

A couple going through a divorce who don't want the neighborhood speculating before the kids have been told. A family selling a parent's home during probate who'd rather not field casual offers at the grocery store. A business owner whose employees might read a listing as a sign the company is leaving town. Someone relocating for a job that isn't public yet. A homeowner whose safety or privacy situation makes a front-yard sign and open-house foot traffic a genuine problem, not just an annoyance.

What these situations share isn't secrecy for its own sake. It's that the seller has something at stake beyond the sale price — a timeline, a relationship, a negotiation, or a piece of personal safety — that public exposure can damage.

If any of those sound familiar, the standard playbook needs modifying before your home ever touches the market.

What discretion looks like in practice

A quiet sale isn't just "no sign in the yard." It's a set of deliberate decisions made before the first buyer ever hears the address.

Pre-market preparation without neighborhood chatter. Photography, repairs, staging, and pricing work can all happen without broadcasting intent. Contractors get scheduled thoughtfully. There's no "coming soon" tease building buzz you don't want. The home gets fully ready in private, so when it does surface, it surfaces finished — no half-dressed listing sitting exposed while the work catches up.

Controlled showings. Instead of open houses and lockbox traffic, showings happen by appointment with vetted, pre-qualified buyers — people who have demonstrated they can actually perform, accompanied by their agent, at times the seller controls. Fewer showings, higher quality, no strangers wandering through your home out of curiosity.

Information that never leaks. This is the piece most people miss. Your reasons for selling, your timeline, your bottom line — every one of those is negotiating leverage, and in a normal sale they leak constantly. The neighbor mentions your divorce to a buyer's agent. A chatty conversation at a showing reveals you've already bought elsewhere. In a disciplined sale, the answer to "why are they selling?" is simple and boring, every time: the home is for sale, the price is the price, and offers will be evaluated on their merits. Nothing else moves across the table.

A smaller, deliberate audience. Sometimes that means marketing the home quietly to a targeted pool of qualified buyers and agents before — or instead of — full public exposure. There are real trade-offs here: a smaller audience can mean fewer competing offers, and that's a conversation to have honestly, with numbers, before choosing the approach. Discretion has a price. So does exposure. The right answer depends on what you're protecting.

Discretion is not the same as underselling

Let me be direct about the objection, because it's a fair one: doesn't limiting exposure cost you money?

It can — if it's done lazily. A quiet sale done right compensates with preparation and precision. The home is priced from real comparable data, not hope. The buyer pool is smaller but serious — no tire-kickers, no curiosity tours. And the negotiation happens from a position of strength, because the other side of the table knows nothing about your pressure, your timeline, or your reasons.

I've watched sellers with every advantage give it away in casual conversation, and I've watched disciplined sellers protect value simply by controlling what left the room. In my experience, information leaks cost sellers more than small audiences do.

The goal is never secrecy for its own sake. The goal is that you decide what the market knows about you — instead of finding out later what it already knew.

The habit behind it

People sometimes ask why I care this much about information handling in what is, on paper, a residential real estate practice in the Flathead Valley.

The honest answer: old habits, good habits. When you've worked in environments where managing information protected people, you don't switch it off because the setting changed. A client's situation — their divorce, their estate, their finances, their reasons — belongs to them. It isn't content, it isn't gossip, and it isn't leverage for the other side. That's true on every sale I take, whether it's a quiet one or a front-page one.

Discretion, it turns out, isn't a special service. It's just how the job should be done.

So here's the question worth sitting with: if you sold your home this year, is there anything — a timeline, a situation, a reason — you'd rather the market not know? If the answer is yes, the time to plan for that is before the first phone call gets made, not after.

item.title: Keep the House or Sell It? The Montana Divorce Buyout, Explained
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: One spouse wants to stay in the house. Here's what a divorce buyout actually requires in Montana — valuation, refinancing, and the equity math — and how to tell when selling is the better outcome for both people.
item.content:encoded:
Keep the House or Sell It? The Montana Divorce Buyout, Explained

If you're going through a divorce in the Flathead Valley and one of you wants to keep the house, you've probably already had some version of this conversation: "You keep the house, I'll take my share, and we move on."

It sounds simple. It's usually the most complicated financial move in the entire divorce.

Here's what most people get wrong about buyouts: they think the hard part is agreeing to it. The hard part is executing it. A buyout is really three separate problems — agreeing on what the house is worth, getting one name off the mortgage, and finding the money to pay out the other person's share. Miss any one of the three, and the deal that sounded so clean in the kitchen falls apart months later, usually at the worst possible time.

Let's walk through each one, so you can tell early whether a buyout actually pencils for your situation — or whether selling is the kinder path for both of you.

Problem one: what is the house actually worth?

Everything downstream depends on this number, and it's the first place buyouts go sideways.

The spouse keeping the house has every incentive to see a lower value. The spouse being bought out has every incentive to see a higher one. Zillow doesn't settle it — automated estimates in a market like ours, with everything from in-town Kalispell homes to acreage properties with wells and shops, can miss by a wide margin.

What typically works: a professional appraisal, or sometimes two, with a method for reconciling them agreed on in advance. Some couples use a broker price opinion as a starting point and an appraisal to finalize. The specific mechanism matters less than agreeing on the mechanism before you see the number. Once a number is on the table, neutrality gets a lot harder.

One more wrinkle worth knowing: in a divorce settlement, the buyout price is negotiable in a way the open market isn't. Some couples discount slightly from appraised value to reflect the selling costs a real sale would have carried. That's a conversation for your attorneys — but know that it's a lever.

Problem two: the refinance nobody budgets for

Here's the part that quietly kills more buyouts than the valuation fight ever does.

Agreeing that one spouse keeps the house does not take the other spouse off the mortgage. The lender isn't a party to your divorce decree. If both names are on the note, both of you remain fully liable — even after the decree says the house belongs to one of you. The only clean way off the note is a refinance in the keeping spouse's name alone (or, occasionally, a loan assumption if the loan allows it — ask the servicer, and don't assume).

That means the spouse keeping the house has to qualify for the mortgage by themselves — one income, and often a larger loan than the original, because the refinance frequently has to pull out cash to fund the equity payment. Qualifying solo at today's rates, for a bigger loan, on one income, right after a divorce has split the household finances in half: that's the test. A meaningful number of people don't pass it.

If you're the spouse being bought out, this matters just as much. Never let the decree say "spouse keeps the house and will refinance eventually." Insist on a deadline — commonly 90 to 180 days — with an automatic sale provision if the refinance doesn't happen. Your attorney will have language for this. Without it, your name can stay on that note for years, dragging on your credit and your ability to buy your own next home.

Problem three: where does the equity payment come from?

Flathead Valley homeowners who bought before the run-up are often sitting on substantial equity. That's good news and bad news in a buyout: there's real money to divide, and real money that has to come from somewhere.

The usual sources are cash-out proceeds from the refinance, offsetting assets — one spouse takes the house, the other takes retirement accounts or other property of comparable value — or some combination. Offsetting sounds tidy, but a dollar of home equity and a dollar in a retirement account aren't the same dollar once taxes and access rules enter the picture. This is exactly where "consult your attorney and your CPA" isn't a disclaimer — it's the actual advice.

When the buyout doesn't pencil — and what that means

Run the three tests honestly. Can you agree on a value? Can the keeping spouse qualify alone? Is there a real source for the equity payment? If any answer is no, the buyout doesn't pencil — and it's far better to know that now than after months of fighting for a house you can't actually afford to keep.

And here's the reframe worth sitting with: selling isn't losing. A sale converts the fight into a number, splits it cleanly, gets both names off the debt on day one, and lets two people start their next chapter with cash instead of entanglement. I've watched buyouts succeed and I've watched them strain budgets for years. Sometimes the house one spouse "won" becomes the anchor that keeps the divorce from ever really ending.

There's no judgment in either answer. The goal is a decision made on numbers, early, instead of emotion, late.

A question to sit with

If you're facing this decision, ask yourself: am I trying to keep the house, or am I trying to keep what the house represents? Those are different things, and only one of them can be refinanced.

item.title: Kalispell & Whitefish Market Update: The August Turn
item.dc:creator: Ryan Berner
item.description: New listings in Kalispell just dropped 36% in a month, days on market are stretching, and the 30-year rate hit 6.66%. Here's what the August turn means if you're listing or writing offers in the Flathead Valley right now.
item.content:encoded:
Every year, right around the first week of August, the Flathead Valley market makes a quiet pivot. Nobody rings a bell. The lake is still busy, Glacier traffic is still backed up at West Glacier, and the listing photos still look like postcards. But underneath, the numbers start moving in a different direction — and if you're listing a home or writing an offer this month, you want to see the turn before everyone else does.

It's Monday, so let's do numbers first, then the read.

The Numbers: Early August 2026

Here's what the most recent data shows for Kalispell and the surrounding market, covering roughly July 2 through August 2, 2026 (source: Montana Regional MLS data via IDEAL Real Estate's Kalispell market report, July 2026 period):

New listings came in at just 97 for the period — down 36.6% from June. That's the sharpest one-month pullback in fresh inventory we've seen all season.

Active listings sat at 525, down 3.67% from June. Total inventory has crested. The summer stack of homes is no longer growing — it's starting to thin as listings expire, withdraw, or go under contract without being replaced.

Average days on market for active listings stretched to 106, up more than 10% from June. The homes still sitting are sitting longer.

Average asking price per square foot slipped to $367, down about 1.8% — small, but it's the direction that matters. Sellers are starting to reach down toward the market instead of over it.

For context on closed sales: Kalispell's median sale price was $627,495 in June 2026, with sold properties averaging around 58 days on market (source: Movoto market trends, June 2026 data). Notice the gap — homes that actually sell move in about two months. The active inventory averaging 106 days? That's the overpriced tail.

And rates: the Freddie Mac Primary Mortgage Market Survey put the 30-year fixed at 6.66% as of July 30, 2026, up from 6.58% the week before, with the 15-year at 6.04% (source: Freddie Mac PMMS, July 30, 2026). That's the highest reading in nearly a year.

What the Turn Actually Is

Put those numbers together and you get the August pattern I see every year in this valley:

Sellers stop entering the market. The 36% drop in new listings isn't weakness — it's the calendar. Families who wanted to move before school starts have already listed. Anyone thinking "maybe next spring" has decided to wait. The window for fresh competition is closing.

Buyer traffic thins, but it changes character. The July crowds — half of them tourists dreaming through open houses between huckleberry stops — head home. Who's left in August and September? People who need to buy. Relocations, job starts, 1031 deadlines, life changes. Fewer showings, better showings.

The overpriced tail gets exposed. When homes are selling in 58 days and yours has been active for 100+, the market has already voted. In July, a seller could tell themselves the right buyer just hadn't come through yet. In August, that story stops holding.

If You're Selling This Month

Two very different situations, two very different plays.

If you're already on the market and past 60 days: you're now chasing the market, and the worst version of that is the slow drip — $10,000 off every three weeks, trailing buyer expectations the whole way down. If you're going to adjust, adjust once, decisively, to a number that's inside the market instead of just closer to it. One meaningful correction in early August beats three timid ones through October.

If you're about to list: the turn is actually your friend. You're entering a market where new competition just dropped by a third and the remaining buyers are serious. A home that's priced against June's closed sales — not against your neighbor's hopeful asking price — can stand out sharply right now precisely because so much of the active inventory is stale. Preparation still matters more than timing: inspection-ready condition and honest pricing beat any calendar trick.

If You're Buying This Month

Rates at 6.66% sting, no question. But look at what you're getting in exchange: sellers with 100+ days on market, softening asking prices per square foot, and a thinning pool of competing buyers. August through September is historically when Flathead Valley buyers get concessions that were unthinkable in June — price adjustments, rate buydowns, inspection repairs actually negotiated instead of waived.

The move is to be selective and decisive at the same time. On stale listings, the data is your leverage — days on market and the asking-to-sold gap justify a serious-but-under-ask offer. On well-priced fresh listings, don't get cute: the good ones still go, because every other serious buyer in the valley is watching the same shrinking pool of new inventory you are.

And on rates: marry the house, date the rate is a cliché, but run the actual math with your lender on what a future refinance would look like before you let 6.66% talk you out of a home that fits.

The Bottom Line

The August turn isn't a downturn — it's a changing of the guard. Casual sellers and casual buyers leave the field. What's left is a smaller, more serious market where preparation and pricing discipline decide outcomes. That's not a market to fear. That's a market to plan for.
